proposition: For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 50, the sum of k^3 for k = 1..n equals (n(n+1)/2)^2.
hypotheses: the sum is empty for n = 0

argument.text: The identity holds at n = 1: the left side is 1 and the right side evaluates to 1.
Write F(n) = (n(n+1)/2)^2. For every n with 1 <= n <= 49, F(n+1) - F(n) = (n+1)^3, which is exactly the term added when the upper limit increases by one.
Put H(n) = n^2 + [n = 3]. Then (n-3)n^2 = (n-3)H(n) for every n in [1, 50].
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 50: if n is divisible by 4 then n(n+1)/2 is even.
Every integer n in [1, 50] is even or odd, so the two cases below are exhaustive.
Let G(n) = F(n) + [n = 3]. Then (n-3)F(n) = (n-3)G(n) for every n in [1, 50].
For every integer n with 2 <= n <= 50 we have n^2 >= 2n.
For every integer n with 1 <= n <= 50, n^3 is congruent to n modulo 6.
Base case and increment together establish the identity for every n in [1, 50].
